title: Chapter 33.  Current Developments — The Statehood Debate & Situation Today (2024-2026)

blocks.content: This chapter brings the constitutional-status narrative (Chapters 13-16) fully up to date with the single most important LIVE current-affairs issue for J&K as of 2026: the still-pending restoration of full statehood, a promise made by the Union Government but not yet fulfilled as of this writing. This is presented as an open, ongoing political-administrative question rather than a settled fact.
The Statehood Promise & Its Status as of 2026

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The statehood debate centers on political promises and status updates during the 2024-2026 period.
Multiple opposing and supporting arguments define the ongoing discourse over statehood restoration.
Security and normalcy trends serve as critical benchmarks for evaluating ground conditions.

blocks.content: When the Government of India abrogated Article 370 and reorganised the state into two Union Territories in August 2019, Union Home Minister Amit Shah stated in Parliament that J&K's statehood would be restored 'at an appropriate time', once conditions (particularly the security situation) were judged suitable — a commitment reiterated by the government before the Supreme Court during the 2023 constitutional challenge proceedings (Chapter 13).

The Supreme Court's December 2023 judgment, while upholding the abrogation's validity, explicitly directed that J&K's statehood 'should be restored at the earliest' as a step, though it stopped short of fixing a specific deadline for this restoration (unlike the Assembly-election deadline of 30 September 2024, which the Court did fix and which was duly met, per Chapter 16).
Current Developments — The Statehood Debate & Situation Today (2024-2026)

As of 2026, more than two years after the December 2023 judgment and well over a year after the elected Omar Abdullah government took office (October 2024), statehood has NOT yet been restored. Chief Minister Omar Abdullah and his government have repeatedly and publicly renewed calls for restoration, describing the current Union Territory arrangement as a 'temporary phase' and citing the practical governance difficulties of what they describe as a 'dual power structure' between the elected government and the centrally-appointed Lieutenant Governor, who retains significant reserved powers (including over matters such as land, police and public order — a structural arrangement broadly comparable to Delhi's framework, covered in the companion Delhi GS volume).

cells: Union Home Minister Amit Shah tells Parliament statehood will be restored 'at an appropriate time'
Supreme Court upholds Article 370 abrogation; directs statehood restoration 'at the earliest' without fixing a specific deadline
Omar Abdullah's elected government takes office; immediately begins pressing for statehood restoration as a priority

Repeated public statements from Union ministers reaffirm the commitment to eventual restoration without providing a timeline; J&K political parties (NC, Congress, and others) continue public advocacy, including protests

Statehood remains unrestored; the matter is before the Supreme Court again via fresh petitions seeking a time-bound directive; the J&K government continues to press the issue publicly, including hopes expressed around Independence Day 2026 for restoration by the following year's Independence Day

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: The single most important thing to know about this topic for current-affairs purposes: statehood restoration was PROMISED (by the Union Government, in Parliament and before the Supreme Court) but has NOT YET HAPPENED as of 2026 — present this as an unresolved, actively debated issue rather than describing J&K as having already regained full state status.
Arguments on Different Sides of the Debate

items: Those calling for prompt restoration (including the ruling NC-Congress coalition in J&K, most opposition parties, and various civil-society/legal petitioners before the Supreme Court) argue that continued UT status without full statehood undermines cooperative federalism and the democratic mandate of J&K's elected government, creates governance confusion from the 'dual power structure' between the LG and the Chief Minister, and that the successful, peaceful conduct of the 2024 Assembly elections demonstrates the security situation no longer justifies withholding statehood.

The Union Government's position, as articulated by senior ministers, is that statehood will be restored once conditions are judged appropriate, without committing to a specific timeline, citing continued security sensitivities (including occasional border/infiltration-related incidents) as grounds for a cautious, phased approach; officials have also periodically pointed to ongoing 'business rules' negotiations (reportedly covering the allocation of specific administrative powers/ministries between the LG and the elected government) as an intermediate step short of full statehood.

Economic and social indicators cited in various public commentary — including J&K's per-capita income (reported in the UT's own 2025-26 Economic Survey as below the national average) and unemployment figures above the national average, particularly among graduates — have been invoked by different commentators either as evidence that continued central oversight remains necessary, or conversely as evidence that greater local self-governance and accountability (via full statehood) is needed to address these challenges more effectively.
Competitive exams often question the timeline and legal/political aspects of the statehood debate (2024-2026).
Be prepared to evaluate arguments on different sides of statehood restoration.
Understand the key indicators used to measure security and normalcy trends.

The period since 2019 has generally seen a reported decline in large-scale organised militancy-related violence compared to earlier decades (Chapter 12), alongside government emphasis on infrastructure development, tourism recovery, and events such as the 2023 G20-linked meeting in Srinagar (Chapter 23) as markers of improved normalcy.

At the same time, independent and civil-society commentary has continued to flag concerns around the continued use of preventive-detention laws (the Public Safety Act, Chapter 12), periodic internet/communications restrictions during specific security situations, and restrictions on some forms of political protest and civil-society activity — concerns that form part of the broader, still-live debate over the pace and adequacy of the region's return to full normalcy.

Both the positive developments (successful elections, infrastructure completion, tourism recovery) and the continuing concerns are part of the genuine, actively contested current picture — candidates should present both strands factually rather than asserting a single, settled narrative either way.
J&K statehood was promised by the Union Government (2019 Parliament statement; reaffirmed before the SC) but remained UNRESTORED as of 2026 — an actively live, unresolved issue.
December 2023 SC judgment: upheld Article 370 abrogation; directed statehood restoration 'at the earliest' WITHOUT a fixed deadline (unlike the fixed Sept 2024 election deadline, which was met).
CM Omar Abdullah has repeatedly called the current UT status a 'temporary phase' and pressed for restoration; fresh Supreme Court petitions on the issue were pending as of 2026.

J&K's 2025-26 Economic Survey reported per-capita income below the national average and above-national-average unemployment (especially graduate unemployment) — cited by different sides in the statehood debate.

Security situation shows a general post-2019 decline in large-scale militancy alongside continued use of preventive-detention laws and periodic restrictions — both strands are part of the actively debated current picture.
